title: Maddi in the forest
hookLine: Vessantara's wife comes home with fruit to find her children gone (Jataka 547)

cards: A basket of fruit, roots and leaves, heavy on her hip. Maddi has been gathering in the forest all day, the way she does every day, so her children will have something to eat when she gets home.
The night before, she slept badly, troubled by a frightening dream, and she told her husband about it. He told her not to worry. Now the light is going, and she is late.
Something keeps standing in her path.

teach.h: A LION, A TIGER, A LEOPARD.
teach.b: A lion, a tiger and a leopard stand across her road and won't move. The tale tells us what Maddi doesn't know: they're gods in animal shape, holding her back so she can't come home in the middle of the gift.
She pleads with them, and only at nightfall do they step aside. Every evening the children run out to meet her.
Tonight nobody runs. She calls their names. She looks where they played, by the pond, under the trees.
Vessantara, sitting there, at first says nothing.
Maddi searches the whole night through, and at dawn she falls at her husband's feet as if dead.
He sprinkles water on her face to bring her round, and only then tells her: he has given the children away to a brahmin, so that he might reach awakening.
The tale has her rejoice in the gift, and join her merit to his. Some readers find that ending hard to accept. Others hear in it a love already tested by the worst night of her life.
The tale does not hurry past her grief. It gives her search room to breathe, line after line, place after place.
Tradition says that where the whole tale is recited aloud at festivals, Maddi's search is a part listeners wait for, and weep through.
A story told for the sake of generosity stops, for a long time, to stand beside a mother looking for her children in the dark.

how: Where the Vessantara tale is recited aloud, Maddi's chapter may be chanted slowly and with feeling, and audiences listen to it as part of a merit-making festival.

games.q: you're Maddi, late and loaded with fruit. a lion, a tiger and a leopard stand across the path home, and night is falling. what do you do?
o: go back into the forest and wait for morning.
plead with them to let you go home.
games.why: she pleads with them. they are gods in animal shape, holding her back so she can't interrupt the gift, and they step aside only at nightfall.

practice: In Maddi's tale, love looks like worry. Bring to mind a time someone who cared for you worried about you: a night they waited up, a face at the door when you finally got home, and look at it now as care with nowhere else to go.
If that relationship is a painful one, choose anyone whose care reached you.

wordCard.voice: Maddi. The mother who came home with fruit and searched all night for her children. Today's word.
